extraction.name: Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images
extraction.description: Paper describing training generative models and classifiers on the Tiny Images dataset, including CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 label subsets, and an algorithm for parallelizing RBM training.
extraction.creator: Alex Krizhevsky
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Groups at MIT and NYU collected a dataset of millions of tiny colour images from the web over the span of six months by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in WordNet, using several search engines including Google, Flickr, and AltaVista, keeping roughly the first 3000 results for each search term, and removing perfect duplicates and images with an excessively large portion of white pixels. The authors also paid students to label a subset of the dataset by filtering mislabeled images for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper states that the tiny images dataset had no reliable class labels and that the search-term labels were extremely unreliable.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: 80 million color images downscaled to 32x32 collected from the web across 79,000 search terms; labeled subsets of 10 classes with 6,000 images per class for CIFAR-10 and 100 classes with 600 images per class for CIFAR-100.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Over the span of six months
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32. Perfect duplicates and images with an excessively large portion of white pixels were removed. For CIFAR-10, duplicate images were also removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a liberal rejection threshold to capture perfect duplicates, re-saved JPEGs, and similar duplicates.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The data were whitened using ZCA whitening; in some experiments the 1000 least significant principal components were deleted; some experiments used 8x8 patches or 8x8 subsampled versions of the 32x32 images; for unwhitened data, the visible-unit standard deviation was set to the average pixel standard deviation (69) and later learned.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Students were paid to label a subset of the tiny images dataset. Each labeler was assigned a class and asked to examine images found with that class as the search term and with hyponyms of the main search term. Labelers rejected images that did not belong to the assigned class according to criteria in the instruction sheet. The authors personally verified every label submitted.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper notes that the original search-term labels were noisy and unreliable. For the labeled subset, the authors personally verified every submitted label. The instruction sheet emphasizes rejecting false positives and handling duplicates later.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Students paid to label the data; no further demographics are provided.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: No sensitive human attributes are described as collected in the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper discusses object recognition and feature learning for natural images and notes that the labeled subset can be used for classification; no broader social impact discussion is provided.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is biased by web search collection using English nouns and search engines, and the paper notes that search-term labels are extremely unreliable. The labeled subset also reflects the chosen object classes and excludes some ambiguous categories such as pickup trucks from automobile and truck.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The tiny images dataset has unreliable labels, and the paper notes that it is difficult to use for object recognition without creating reliable labels. The whitening transformation may exaggerate some noisy directions, and the reconstruction error is not a very good measure of model fit because it depends heavily on Markov chain mixing.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Unsupervised training of deep generative models, pre-training features for object recognition, and classification experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The paper also uses the labeled subset for training, validation/test evaluation, and fine-tuning neural networks initialized from RBM features.
